content: A hairball is a compact mass of hair or fur that forms in the stomach of animals and is sometimes expelled through vomiting when it grows too large. These hairballs are typically elongated, tightly packed cylinders of fur, but they may also contain fragments of ingested food or other materials. Hairballs can sometimes be misdiagnosed as other gastrointestinal conditions, such as lymphosarcoma, tuberculosis, or splenic tumors. Cats are particularly susceptible to hairball formation due to their grooming habits, during which they ingest fur by licking their coats. Rabbits are also prone to hairballs because they groom themselves in a similar manner to cats. However, hairballs pose a greater risk to rabbits because they are unable to regurgitate them. Given the delicate nature of a rabbit’s digestive system, untreated hairballs can lead to anorexia, dehydration, and potentially death. Cattle are another species known to develop hairballs, but since they cannot vomit, these masses are usually discovered post-mortem and can grow to significant sizes. In clinical terms, a trichobezoar is a type of bezoar—a mass trapped in the gastrointestinal tract—formed from ingested hair. Trichobezoars are often associated with trichotillomania, a compulsive hair-pulling disorder. Although rare, they can be life-threatening if not identified and treated, often requiring surgical removal. In humans, hairballs are uncommon but have been documented. They form when strands of hair accumulate in the stomach and cannot be expelled due to friction against the gastric mucosa. Hairballs are frequently observed in young females with trichophagia (hair-eating), trichotillomania, or pica. Notable cases include the surgical removal of a 3-kilogram hairball from a patient’s lower intestine and a 9-pound hairball extracted from the stomach of an 18-year-old in Kyrgyzstan in 2014. Hairballs in humans can be particularly dangerous because hair is indigestible and cannot pass through the gastrointestinal system. Even vomiting may fail to expel the hair mass, leading to significant impairment of digestive function.
